literature.headline_zh: 人肠道病毒本期文献呈现多方向研究进展
literature.lead_zh: 本期人肠道病毒研究集中呈现以下进展。
key_findings_zh: 44 个国家报告了 8184 例 EV-D68 病例,其中 267 例 (3·3%) 是各大洲 26 个国家报告的与 EV-D68 相关的急性弛缓性麻痹病例。EV-D68 仍然与严重呼吸道疾病和 急性弛缓性脊髓炎 相关,不仅主要发生在五岁以下的儿童中,而且在成人中也越来越多。 [10.1016/j.lanmic.2026.101570]
磷脂合成的增加消耗内源和外源的长链脂肪酸(LCFA)。中性脂质合成的抑制促进了 LCFA 重新定位到受感染细胞的膜上,并增加了它们的抗病毒效力。 [10.1128/jvi.00902-26]
鉴定出针对 p37 的亚微摩尔效力化合物,并发现 Jun14135 和 Jun14934 对多种 EV-D68 菌株具有广谱 抗病毒药物 活性。 [10.7282/t3-mfq6-xt72]
literature.trend_or_risk_zh: 本期研究方向以入选文献实际覆盖的临床、流行病学、宿主生态、诊断或分子监测主题为准。
literature.lead_en: This reporting window highlights the following research developments.
key_findings_en: 8184 EV-D68 cases were reported by 44 countries, and 267 (3·3%) of these cases were EV-D68-associated acute flaccid paralysis cases reported by 26 countries, across all continents. [10.1016/j.lanmic.2026.101570]

The increased phospholipid synthesis consumes endogenously and exogenously derived long-chain fatty acids (LCFA). The inhibition of neutral lipid synthesis promoted LCFAs retargeting to the membranes in infected cells and increased their anti-viral potency. [10.1128/jvi.00902-26]

Sub-micromolar potency compounds targeting p37 were identified, and Jun14135 and Jun14934 were found to have broad-spectrum antiviral activity against multiple strains of EV-D68. [10.7282/t3-mfq6-xt72]
literature.trend_or_risk_en: The direction of this week's research is defined by the clinical, epidemiological, ecological, diagnostic and molecular topics actually represented by the eligible publications.
literature.brief_en: This literature brief prioritizes papers published in the active reporting window and ranks them by relevance, evidence availability, study quality, recency, and independent-source convergence. Detailed study-specific evidence is retained in the article cards below.

papers.title: Global epidemiology and genetic evolution of enterovirus D68 over a decade (2015-24): a systematic review.
papers.abstract: Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) is a persistent global health concern, causing mild to severe respiratory disease and, in rare cases, acute flaccid myelitis, a polio-like paralytic syndrome. In this systematic review, we synthesised global data on the epidemiology and genetic evolution of EV-D68 from 2015 to 2024 and show its continued widespread circulation and concerning severity. 8184 EV-D68 cases were reported by 44 countries, and 267 (3·3%) of these cases were EV-D68-associated acute flaccid paralysis cases reported by 26 countries, across all continents. Biennial upsurges followed a distinct every-even-year pattern until 2020, after which the circulation showed geographical diversification in Europe and North America, possibly influenced by the COVID-19 pandemic. EV-D68 remained associated with severe respiratory disease and acute flaccid myelitis, not only primarily in children younger than five years but also increasingly in adults. Individuals who progressed to acute flaccid paralysis had poor prognosis for full recovery. Genotypic shifts were marked by the dominance of subgenotype B3 since 2016 and A2/D since 2018, with novel variants emerging for both after 2020. Despite limitations in surveillance quality and coverage, the findings underscore the need for sustained surveillance, improved diagnostic strategies, and targeted interventions to mitigate EV-D68-related morbidity.

papers.title: Infection-specific long-chain fatty acid metabolism as a broad anti-enterovirus target
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Enteroviruses are arguably the most numerous group of viruses infecting humans. While most enterovirus infections are benign and self-resolving, their sheer number inevitably increases the chances of multiple complications. The diversity of enteroviruses means that the development of vaccines is only economically feasible against a select few, and no direct-acting or host-targeted anti-virals are approved to treat enteroviral infections, largely due to the rapid development of resistance against all experimental drugs. Here, we explored a universal property of enterovirus infection—a massive upregulation of phospholipid synthesis as a target for anti-viral interventions. The increased phospholipid synthesis consumes endogenously and exogenously derived long-chain fatty acids (LCFA). We demonstrate that polyunsaturated LCFAs can have a broad anti-enteroviral effect, affecting multiple steps of the virus life cycle. The anti-viral activity of LCFAs did not strictly depend on the degree of unsaturation or their capacity to induce lipid peroxidation, but significantly correlated with their conformation. This suggests that their incorporation into the phospholipid molecules makes the replication organelle membranes incapable of properly accommodating viral replication machinery. Accordingly, the inhibition of neutral lipid synthesis promoted LCFAs retargeting to the membranes in infected cells and increased their anti-viral potency. We show that this approach is effective against diverse enteroviruses in different cell types, including differentiated primary cells, and that attempts to establish viruses resistant to such treatment were unsuccessful. IMPORTANCE Humans are hosts to more than 300 distinct enteroviruses. Enterovirus infections can induce multiple short-term and long-term complications, including such serious conditions as paralysis, myocarditis, aseptic meningitis, and others. Yet, licensed vaccines are available only against poliovirus and enterovirus A71, and no specific anti-enterovirus drugs are approved for clinical practice. These viruses rapidly develop resistance to either virus- or host-acting experimental compounds. We explored a shared feature of enterovirus infection, a strong upregulation of phospholipid synthesis in infected cells, as a tool to control enterovirus replication. By altering the long-chain fatty acids composition available to infected cells, replication of diverse enteroviruses can be similarly suppressed, and the selection of resistant mutants was not successful. Thus, targeting infection-induced changes in cellular lipid metabolism, rather than individual viral or host factors, may offer a promising approach for controlling enterovirus infections.

papers.title: Development of Therapeutics for Orthopoxvirus and Enterovirus infections: Small Molecule Antiviral Drug Discovery and Library Generation
papers.abstract: Endemic diseases have the potential to spread quickly and overwhelm vulnerable populations, leading to the necessity for antiviral drugs to treat infections. This work focuses on the development of antivirals for orthopoxviruses and enteroviruses, as well as compound library development. Orthopoxviruses, which include monkeypox virus (mpox), vaccinia virus, and the eradicated smallpox virus, have few approved therapies, with no antiviral drug being approved for mpox infection. The viral p37 protein is a known therapeutic target for poxvirus antivirals. Tecovirimat is a known p37 inhibitor; however, it did not effectively treat mpox infections in clinical trials. Tecovirimat contains a large hydrocarbon motif, and previous changes in this motif have retained some antiviral efficacy. We identified a series of compounds containing amide, hydrazide, and carbamide linkers with adamantane, noradamantane, and other cyclic hydrocarbon substitutions with sub-micromolar potency targeting p37. The second focus of this work was the development of antivirals targeting Enterovirus-D68 (EV-D68). EV-D68 is an upper respiratory virus associated with polio-like acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) and primarily represents a threat to children under 16. Currently, there is no vaccine or Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved drug to combat EV-D68 infections. We used high-throughput screening to identify a promising hit molecule that we further optimized. We identified that the target was the VP1 capsid protein. We identified candidates Jun14135 and Jun14934 having broad-spectrum antiviral activity against multiple strains of EV-D68. Furthermore, we identified the potential for co-therapy opportunities of Jun16934 with the EV-D68 2C inhibitor Jun6504. Finally, we look to improve the speed of preclinical development for covalent inhibitors by developing a direct-to-biology (D2B) methodology to quickly synthesize molecules for screening. D2B is being increasingly utilized by both industry and academia, primarily due to the potential to save both time and cost by using small amounts of crude reactions for use in biological assays.

papers.source_body_en: Endemic diseases have the potential to spread quickly and overwhelm vulnerable populations, leading to the necessity for antiviral drugs to treat infections. This work focuses on the development of antivirals for orthopoxviruses and enteroviruses, as well as compound library development. Orthopoxviruses, which include monkeypox virus (mpox), vaccinia virus, and the eradicated smallpox virus, have few approved therapies, with no antiviral drug being approved for mpox infection. The viral p37 protein is a known therapeutic target for poxvirus antivirals. Tecovirimat is a known p37 inhibitor; however, it did not effectively treat mpox infections in clinical trials. Tecovirimat contains a large hydrocarbon motif, and previous changes in this motif have retained some antiviral efficacy. We identified a series of compounds containing amide, hydrazide, and carbamide linkers with adamantane, noradamantane, and other cyclic hydrocarbon substitutions with sub-micromolar potency targeting p37. The second focus of this work was the development of antivirals targeting Enterovirus-D68 (EV-D68). EV-D68 is an upper respiratory virus associated with polio-like acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) and primarily represents a threat to children under 16. Currently, there is no vaccine or Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved drug to combat EV-D68 infections. We used high-throughput screening to identify a promising hit molecule that we further optimized. We identified that the target was the VP1 capsid protein. We identified candidates Jun14135 and Jun14934 having broad-spectrum antiviral activity against multiple strains of EV-D68. Furthermore, we identified the potential for co-therapy opportunities of Jun16934 with the EV-D68 2C inhibitor Jun6504. Finally, we look to improve the speed of preclinical development for covalent inhibitors by developing a direct-to-biology (D2B) methodology to quickly synthesize molecules for screening. D2B is being increasingly utilized by both industry and academia, primarily due to the potential to save both time and cost by using small amounts of crude reactions for use in biological assays.

news.content: Mutated flu strain pushes virus past last year's peak in SF The Bay Area is facing a surge in multiple viruses ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday as cold and flu season kicks off with a vengeance. Seasonal flu activity has been high in the Bay Area for weeks, leading to an early start to the flu season. Normally flu activity peaks in December or January, but the San Francisco Public Health Department reported Saturday the rate of positive flu tests had already surpassed last year's peak with signs it could keep climbing. The rate of flu hospitalizations in the city has essentially tied the peak of the most recent flu season. Wastewater shows high level of the flu virus for virtually every Bay Area test location except for the Sunnyvale wastewater treatment plant, which shows medium levels. Dr. Peter Chin-Hong, an infectious disease specialist and a professor of medicine at UC San Francisco, said the H1N1 flu variant or so-called swine flu is the primary driver of infections right now, and the virus has a new mutation called G155E that may be causing the increase in infections. "The H1N1 is just a tiny bit different this year, so, it just means that more people are susceptible," he said. Chin-Hong also said that flu activity started picking up in September in the Bay Area with the first death reported on Oct. 1, marking a far earlier start to the season than normally. "It came early, so it was actually before a lot of people would have gotten vaccines by our normal recommendations," he said. "So that could have explained sort of like the early uptake." Chin-Hong said a similar flu virus strain spread through parts of East Asia including Japan and Korea last summer, which could be a reason flu cases arrived in the Bay Area so early, ahead of much of the rest of the country. "I think because of a lot of social connections between California and Asia, we might have seen this first," he said. Dr. Brad Hare, chief of infectious diseases at Kaiser Permanente San Francisco, said travel and gatherings for the Thanksgiving holiday mean a likely bump in viral cases in the upcoming weeks. "Those kind of things just give an opportunity for the virus to be spread from one person to another, so we do typically see increases in cases following holidays and activities like that," Hare said, while stressing that anyone who hasn't received their flu vaccine "should be getting their shots as soon as they can." Hare said anyone with the vaccine can benefit immediately from getting the flu shot, if they're worried about getting sick. "The antibodies begin to ramp up right away and they reach fully protective levels at two weeks," Hare said. He said with such an early start, there's a chance of a "a very drawn-out flu season" as the currently circulating influenza A strain could give way to influenza B strain. "You can get very different versions of influenza in the same season," he said. In addition to flu, other viruses such as COVID-19, enterovirus D68 and the norovirus, also known as "winter vomiting virus," are rising in parts of the Bay Area, according to wastewater data. COVID-19 is seeing another peak after rising in the late summer months. Dr. Matt Willis, an epidemiologist and former public health officer for Marin County, said the virus rising so soon after a peak shows how nationwide trends are impacting California, where cases had been rapidly declining until recently. "It's sort of intersecting with our decline and we're starting to see increased rates," he said of trends outside the state. Enterovirus D68, which is at a high level in San Jose wastewater, causes respiratory symptoms similar to a cold and usually resolves on its own. But in rare cases the virus is linked to a potentially dangerous condition called acute flaccid myelitis. Chin-Hong says parents who notice muscle weakness in children a few weeks after having a cold should take them for medical care and mention their previous illness. Another illness that threatens the Thanksgiving holiday is norovirus, aka "the stomach flu." The disease, which causes gastrointestinal symptoms including vomiting and diarrhea, is at high levels in the wastewater in the western half of San Francisco along with San Jose. Chin-Hong told SFGATE the disease often pops up in winter months even though it's not a respiratory disease. The virus is relatively hardy compared to other diseases and can spread easily in groups. "Hand sanitizer doesn't really kill it," he said. "You need to use soap and water." The disease spreads via contaminated surfaces and can infect a person with just 20-100 microscopic particles. "It's just very super easy to catch," Chin-Hong explained. This article originally published at Mutated flu strain pushes virus past last year's peak in SF

Chin-Hong told SFGATE the disease often pops up in winter months even though it's not a respiratory disease. The virus is relatively hardy compared to other diseases and can spread easily in groups. "Hand sanitizer doesn't really kill it," he said. "You need to use soap and water." The disease spreads via contaminated surfaces and can infect a person with just 20-100 microscopic particles. "It's just very super easy to catch," Chin-Hong explained. This article originally published at Mutated flu strain pushes virus past last year's peak in SF

news.content: The laboratory looks legitimate. Staff at the rural compound include trained microbiologists and virologists. Records show it is run by a recent start-up that has the necessary licences needed to order synthetic genetic material . But below the surface, the company is in fact a front for Kill-9, a dissident group with deep reservations about the political status quo. Inside the compound, the group is working to generate a variation of enterovirus D68, a respiratory illness that can cause anything from mild cold-like symptoms to severe breathing difficulties. The lab technicians here want to engineer their own version that is much more deadly . Not too long ago, this small team would have had to rely on trial and error and years of testing to start seeing results in making the pathogen more lethal, but now they have a powerful new tool on their side: AI . More specifically, an AI protein structure prediction tool that allows them to design what experts call custom protein "origami" to create new biomaterials. They also use a host-pathogen interaction tool that predicts how a new virus will hijack human cells, allowing them to map out contagiousness before ever testing it in a physical lab. Finally, they use a DNA fragment assembly tool that allows them to split long genetic code into smaller, manageable chunks, so they can physically stitch them together in a test tube, letting the enzyme fuse the matching ends together to complete the customised DNA strand. The result is a strain of enterovirus modified to attack the central nervous system, causing paralysis and respiratory failure. The modified strain causes the infection to progress to acute flaccid myelitis, a rare and serious neurological condition that affects the spinal cord, causing sudden muscle weakness and loss of reflexes. The pathogen is so aggressive that this happens in 10 per cent of cases – approximately 200-400 times greater than the rate of respiratory failure from polio. There is no effective vaccine or treatment. Within weeks of the pathogen's development, unusual enterovirus outbreaks are detected in several clusters across a number of cities. Cases quickly spread to 13 countries. Hospitals begin running out of ventilators as 54,712 cases and 821 deaths are recorded. Several weeks into the outbreak, with more than 360,000 cases and almost 10,000 deaths, the World Health Organisation declares a pandemic emergency . Just over a year after the outbreak was first detected, a vaccine became available, with the help of AI. By then, more than 850 million had contracted the virus and 60 million people were dead. The story of how this deadly virus was rapidly developed is, of course, a work of fiction. But it is alarmingly close to reality. It was part of a study presented by scientists who are frantically war-gaming how a bioweapon might be created using AI and turned on humans. The results were presented at the Munich Security Conference, one of the world's biggest security conferences, organised by the Nuclear Threat Initiative (NTI). Scientists taking part in the study determined the scenario represented a "realistic threat" and was highly plausible based on current and near-term AI capabilities. The NTI exercise deliberately avoided detailing how the fictional group might disseminate its pathogen, owing to the risk that such information could be misused. Crude examples provided by AI search models suggest pathogens could be dispersed over a city using weather balloons. Other more sophisticated plots mapped out by researchers include distributing viruses to livestock in food supplies, which then infect the meat that humans eat. When Alex Turner, a former researcher, left Google DeepMind he cited its alleged broken promise about selling its system to the US military 'without restrictions against killer robots or mass spying' Recent warnings about the rapid advance of AI have focused on biotechnology, as well as concern over physical weapons that are also being developed at a rapid rate. And so the race is on to build Weapon X: an AI so powerful that, in the wrong hands, it could unlock the means to destroy humanity. "It's hard for an AI to do it on its own right now," says Alex Turner, a former researcher at Google DeepMind who resigned in June over the dangers of the technology. "But if it had that much control, it would be able to synthesise a very dangerous bioweapon, wipe out most of humanity, then clean up what's left with a couple of drone strikes." On Sept 9, Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher at Anthropic, announced he was quitting the industry. In a blistering resignation statement, he accused AI companies of "gambling with our lives", warning that those building the technology "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade". What followed was a worldwide hysteria that has changed the course of AI forever. "Happy Coxon Day to all who will one day celebrate it," declared Eliezer Yudkowsky, a prominent figure in the field. It was the day the world woke up to the growing certainty that the technology being developed to transform human life could also destroy it. In September, Anthropic published research detailing attempts to misuse its Claude models for potentially dangerous biological work. The company acknowledged that its most capable systems had demonstrated capabilities that could provide "meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons". The following month, Sir Ken McCallum, the director general of MI5, warned AI had the potential to "change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons". Terrorists had long sought access to chemical and biological weapons, he said, but the technology could put dangerous knowledge within reach of people who would otherwise lack it. The threat is not confined to biology. AI is already changing the machinery of war. "We are already in the age of AI warfare," says Paul Scharre, executive vice president at the Centre for a New American Security and formerly of the US office of the secretary of defence. AI is increasingly being used to analyse battlefield intelligence, identify potential targets and help military commanders make decisions at speed. In Ukraine, both sides have deployed AI-assisted drones and targeting systems, such as Russia's Lancet drone, while Israel has used AI tools to help identify targets in Gaza. When Mr Turner left Google DeepMind in June, he cited Google's alleged broken promise about selling its system to the US military "without restrictions against killer robots or mass spying". "I left Deepmind because I was concerned about Google selling its AI to the US military in a way that didn't respect the lives of the people around the world, given its potential for irresponsible integration into AI weapons without humans overseeing them," he told The Telegraph. Mr Turner is particularly concerned about weapons that could carry out attacks without a clear chain of human accountability. "AI-piloted weapons that allow killing people in a way that's extremely hard to attribute," he said. So what might Weapon X actually look like? The idea of an AI superweapon will not be a singular physical weapon, but "more like a network of capabilities of smart systems that are able to respond to high level commands, collaborate with each other, and do things with a high level of autonomy", said Vincent Boulanin, director of the Governance of Artificial Intelligence Programme at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. One possible manifestation of this is AI-enabled drone swarms: large groups of unmanned aircraft that use AI to communicate, coordinate their movements and operate as a single system. Zachary Kallenborn, an autonomous weapons and drone swarms analyst, argues such swarms could become weapons of mass destruction. "Drone swarms are potential future weapons of mass destruction," he said. One of the greatest dangers, he argued, is the possibility of errors multiplying as large numbers of autonomous machines operate together. "What happens if one of those drones confuses a school bus for a tank, and then the whole thing potentially goes out of control?" he asked. The technology is already being integrated into the systems used by some of the world's most powerful militaries. The Pentagon's Maven Smart System, developed by defence technology company Palantir, brings together information from sources including satellite imagery, drone footage and radar to help identify and prioritise potential targets. During the first 24 hours of Operation Epic Fury, Maven was used to help process and prioritise more than 1,000 targets across Iran. Anthropic's Claude models were integrated into the system, helping military planners analyse intelligence and accelerate the targeting process. The scale of investment is considerable. The Pentagon's 2026 budget request included $13.4bn (£10.6bn) for autonomy and autonomous systems. US Central Command launched Operation Epic Fury in February 2026 - Getty/Anadolu Mr Scharre has spent years examining the implications of autonomous weapons. He led the US department of defence working group that drafted Directive 3000.09, establishing the Pentagon's policy on autonomy in weapon systems. "In the long run, the dangerous prospect for militaries is that we shift to a world where humans are no longer in control of war in any meaningful way, and the pace and tempo of war occurs at machine speed," he said. Michael Horowitz, a former senior Pentagon official who worked on the US government's approach to autonomous weapons, says the problem has been recognised for decades. "Even in the early days, 15 or 20 years ago, people could see the technology was going towards greater autonomy, and that that was going to raise some really tough questions about the role of humans in warfare," he said. The technology is changing not only how wars are fought, but how quickly decisions about life and death are made, and who makes them. "When I listen to companies like Palantir and what they're selling, we are just very much on track for a Terminator-style scenario," said David Scott Krueger, a professor of Responsible AI. The race to build Weapon X is already under way. The race to stop it is proving considerably harder. There is a fine line between stopping the development of AI altogether and slowing it down safely. For Ed Leon Klinger, chief executive of the AI company Flock, the answer is not for the West to slow its development. "I think we are in a race and I think the worst thing we could possibly do in this race is slow down," he says. If the US and allies hold back, he argues, China could gain an overwhelming advantage, with consequences for Western security and its way of life. Mr Turner, the former Google DeepMind researcher, believes any meaningful attempt to halt the most dangerous developments will have to involve both superpowers. "It seems hard to imagine that this could be stopped without the US and China being very much on board," he says. "They'll have to kind of see that this is a threat to their national security and to their interests." Donald Trump with Xi Jinping as they depart the National Archives Museum following a tour in September - Getty Images/ Win McNamee When Donald Trump met Xi Jinping in September, hopes of an agreement to pause the AI arms race came to nothing. The two sides did agree to establish a dialogue on superintelligence and a communications channel for serious AI-related incidents, but no agreement to slow development emerged. A paper by Andrew Fudenberg, an economics professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and Andrew Koh, a research scientist at Google DeepMind, offers one possible way forward. They propose that companies and governments share information about their progress and agree on where the risks become too great. If each side knew its rivals were not pushing into dangerous territory, the incentive to do so itself would diminish. But that would require a level of transparency and trust that is currently lacking, particularly between Washington and Beijing. In the meantime, governments, scientists and AI companies are taking steps to reduce the risks. Biological weapons are already prohibited under the Biological Weapons Convention. National laws and regulations impose further restrictions, while laboratories operate under strict biosecurity guidelines. AI companies are also introducing safeguards, including testing models for dangerous capabilities and monitoring attempts to misuse them, as outlined in Anthropic's recent report. Kevin Esvelt, an evolutionary biologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said a jailbroken model will instruct a user that the simplest way is to place an infectious virus solution in a medical nebuliser and spray it in the nose of those sleeping in public. "It's hard to imagine us catching someone trying to cause a pandemic like this. We don't really have defences against that," he said. The threat is not confined to biology. AI is already changing the machinery of war.
